content: 1. Weight-for-Age Z-score (WAZ) in Children Consuming Eggs: Iannotti et al. (2017) and Stewart et al. (2019) evaluated the weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in WAZ between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as moderate. 2. Height-for-Age Z-score (HAZ) in Children Consuming Eggs: Iannotti et al. (2017) and Stewart et al. (2019) assessed height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in HAZ between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as low. 3. Weight-for-Height Z-score (WHZ) in Children Consuming Eggs: Iannotti et al. (2017) and Stewart et al. (2019) evaluated weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ) in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in WHZ between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as low. 4. Head Circumference-for-Age Z-score (HCAZ) in Children Consuming Eggs: Stewart et al. (2019) assessed head circumference-for-age z-scores (HCAZ) in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results demonstrated a significant improvement in mean HCAZ among children who consumed eggs compared to those who did not. The quality of evidence was graded as low. 5. Stunting in Children Consuming Eggs: Iannotti et al. (2017) evaluated stunting in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in stunting between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as very low. 6. Anemia in Children Consuming Eggs: Makrides et al. (2002) assessed anemia in breastfed and formula-fed children who consumed four egg yolks per week for six months. The intervention groups included normal and enriched egg yolks, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in anemia prevalence between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as low. 7. Hemoglobin Concentration in Children Consuming Eggs: Makrides et al. (2002) evaluated hemoglobin concentration in breastfed and formula-fed children who consumed four egg yolks per week for six months. The intervention groups included normal and enriched egg yolks, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in hemoglobin concentration between the groups. The quality of evidence was graded as moderate. 8. Serum Ferritin Levels in Children Consuming Eggs: Makrides et al. (2002) assessed serum ferritin levels in breastfed and formula-fed children who consumed four egg yolks per week for six months. The intervention groups included normal and enriched egg yolks, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in serum ferritin levels between the groups. 9. Transferrin Receptors in Children Consuming Eggs: Makrides et al. (2002) evaluated transferrin receptor levels in breastfed and formula-fed children who consumed four egg yolks per week for six months. The intervention groups included normal and enriched egg yolks, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in transferrin receptor levels between the groups. 10. Vitamin B12 Concentration in Children Consuming Eggs: Iannotti et al. (2017) assessed vitamin B12 concentrations in children aged 6–9 months who consumed eggs daily for six months. The intervention group consumed one egg per day, while the control group consumed no eggs. The results showed no significant difference in vitamin B12 concentrations between the groups. 11. Linoleic Acid (LA) in Children Consuming Eggs: Hoffman et al. (2004) evaluated linoleic acid levels in children aged 12 months who consumed dried egg yolks daily for 12 months. The intervention group consumed one jar of study food containing dried egg yolks, while the control group consumed a control food without egg yolks. The results showed no significant difference in mean LA levels between the groups. 12. Docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA) in Children Consuming Eggs: Hoffman et al. (2004) assessed DHA levels in children aged 12 months who consumed dried egg yolks daily for 12 months. The intervention group consumed one jar of study food containing dried egg yolks, while the control group consumed a control food without egg yolks. A significant increase in DHA levels was observed in the intervention group compared to the control group. 13. Eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) in Children Consuming Eggs: Hoffman et al. (2004) evaluated EPA levels in children aged 12 months who consumed dried egg yolks daily for 12 months. The intervention group consumed one jar of study food containing dried egg yolks, while the control group consumed a control food without egg yolks. The results showed no significant difference in mean EPA levels between the groups. 14. Stunting in Children Consuming Caterpillars: Bauserman et al. (2015) assessed stunting in children aged 6–18 months who consumed caterpillar cereal. The intervention group consumed 30–45 g of caterpillar cereal daily, while the control group consumed no caterpillar cereal. The results showed no significant difference in stunting between the groups at any age. The quality of evidence was graded as very low. 15. Wasting in Children Consuming Caterpillars: Bauserman et al. (2015) evaluated wasting in children aged 6–18 months who consumed caterpillar cereal. The intervention group consumed 30–45 g of caterpillar cereal daily, while the control group consumed no caterpillar cereal. The results showed no significant difference in wasting between the groups at any age. The quality of evidence was graded as very low. 16.
